Sibiu, 22 December. Pietro has come for Christmas with Matei, Giulia and Viola to Matei's parents, Doina and Ion. It's his first trip to Romania and his first real snow. He's walking with Ion around the Piața Mare.
It's more beautiful than I thought. Matei said it was small.
It's smaller than Florence, of course. But more than anything it's different. Look at the roofs.
There are eyes! Little windows shaped like eyes.
They're the eyes of the city. People say they watch you. Unlike Florence, here it's the houses that look at you.
And it's colder than I imagined. Minus ten!
The colder it is, the more people stay indoors eating. It's our philosophy.
Like in Florence with ribollita.
Just as you have ribollita, we have sarmale. You'll taste them tomorrow. Doina has been making them for two days.
Are they better than ribollita?
That's a dangerous question. Rather than answer, I'll take you to see the market. Dangerous questions are only asked after mulled wine.

Practical rule: if after "than" comes a simple noun → "di". If anything else comes (adjective, verb, preposition) → "che".

The "non" in "di quanto tu non pensi" is expletive: it negates nothing, it just makes the sentence more elegant. You can leave it out without changing the meaning.

The invitation arrived at the end of November, in a blue envelope with a Romanian stamp, addressed by hand: "Pentru Pietro". Inside was a note from Doina, written in careful and slightly old-fashioned Italian, learned over years of visits to Florence and phone calls with Graziella. "Dear Pietro, this year Matei, Giulia and Viola are coming to Sibiu for Christmas. Ion and I would be happy if you came too. You are fifteen and have never seen real snow, the kind that comes up to your knees. It's time." Pietro read the note three times, then took it to Graziella, who was kneading dough. Graziella read it with floury hands, leaving two white prints on the edges. "Go," she said at once. "But take a proper jacket. And a jar of sauce for Doina. And ask Ion for the sarmale recipe, because she's never wanted to give it to me."

They left on 22 December, at dawn, on a flight from Bologna that landed in Sibiu after two hours. Pietro spent the whole journey with his nose pressed to the window. Below them passed the Alps, then the Hungarian plain, flat and grey, then, suddenly, the Carpathians, covered in snow, white as a sheet spread out in the sun. Viola slept on Giulia's lap. Matei pointed out the mountains to Pietro one by one, with their impossible names. When the plane began to descend, Pietro saw a small city, with red roofs covered in snow and church towers sticking up like pencils. "It's smaller than I thought," he said. Matei smiled. "Wait till you see it up close," he said. "Sibiu is like my mother. From far away it looks simple. Up close you never finish discovering it."

Ion was waiting for them at the airport, in a fur hat and with the old railway pocket watch hanging from his waistcoat, the one he had given Matei when Viola was born and which Matei had given back to him, as promised, when he came back from Malta. He hugged Matei, then Giulia, then picked up Viola, who shouted "Bunicu!" with a perfect Romanian accent. Then he shook Pietro's hand, looked him up and down and said in Italian: "You're taller than I was told." Pietro was one metre eighty-two by now, taller than Matei. "And that jacket is too light," Ion added, taking out of a bag an old grey wool coat. "It was mine when I worked on the Copșa Mică line. Minus twenty, in winter. Put it on." Pietro put it on. It was a little big for him, and smelled of mothballs and tobacco. He wore it for ten days.

On the first afternoon Ion took Pietro for a walk around the centre, while the others rested. It was minus ten. The snow creaked under his shoes, a sound Pietro had never heard, like someone chewing biscuits. In the Piața Mare, the big square, there was the Christmas market: lit wooden huts, the smell of mulled wine and cinnamon, a big wheel, a children's choir singing songs Pietro didn't understand. But what struck him most were the roofs. On the red roofs of the houses, under the snow, there were small windows shaped like half-closed eyes, which seemed to be watching the square. "They're the eyes of the city," Ion explained. "They were there to air the lofts, where grain was kept. But people say they watch you. Unlike Florence, where you look at the houses, here it's the houses that look at you."

That evening, in the little room Doina had prepared for him, with a hand-embroidered quilt and a green tiled stove in the corner, Pietro opened the black notebook and began to write. He wrote everything in the form of comparisons, as came naturally to him. "Sibiu is smaller than Florence, but higher than I thought: the old town is on the hill, the new one below. It's colder here than on the moon. The roofs are steeper than in Florence, so the snow slides off. The houses aren't so much beautiful as curious. People speak more quietly than at home. The bread is darker, the wine sweeter, the coffee longer." He filled two pages. Then he reread them and noticed something strange: in two pages he had described Sibiu only by comparing it with Florence. He hadn't written a single sentence about Sibiu that didn't contain the word "more" or the word "less".

The next day, Doina took everyone to the Brukenthal Museum, the baroque palace on the big square, where a few years earlier Matei had worked on the project with the Uffizi. The director, Mrs Popescu, welcomed them at the door. She had aged, her hair completely white, but she recognised Matei at once and hugged him like a son. Then she led the group through the rooms, to a small sixteenth-century portrait hanging in a corner: a young woman with a blue veil over her hair and two dark, deep eyes that seemed to follow whoever looked at her. Doina stopped in front of the painting and said nothing. Pietro knew the story: that painted woman had the same eyes as Viorica, Doina's mother, who died when Matei was five, the same woman whose photograph now stood on the kitchen shelf in via Maggio, next to Aldo's. Viola, in Matei's arms, pointed at the painting. "Străbunica," she said. Nobody corrected her.

Doina stayed in front of the portrait longer than anyone. When the others had moved away, Pietro saw her moving her lips, softly, without a sound. He went closer and realised she was humming. It was Viorica's lullaby, the one Graziella sang in the trattoria with the wrong accent, the one Viola had recognised at three from the smell of soffritto. Doina noticed, stopped and smiled, a little embarrassed. "My mother sang it to me every evening," she said. "Then she sang it to Matei and Ilinca, when they were little. When she died, I carried on." She pointed at the blue veil in the painting. "She had a headscarf that colour. She wore it on Sundays." At that moment Viola, whom Matei was holding by the hand on the other side of the room, turned round sharply and began to sing the same melody, out loud, with the wrong words and her high voice. The attendant woke up. Nobody told her to stop.

Pietro wandered around the museum for two hours, alone, notebook in hand. The Brukenthal was much smaller than the Uffizi: you could see everything in an afternoon, without queues, without crowds, without people photographing the paintings instead of looking at them. In one room there was only him and an elderly attendant dozing on a chair. In front of a small Flemish landscape, with skaters on a frozen river, Pietro stopped for half an hour. Nobody pushed him, nobody asked him to move. He wrote in the notebook: "The Brukenthal isn't so much big as intimate. At the Uffizi the paintings are more famous, but here they're closer. It's the quietest museum I've ever seen." Then he crossed out "the quietest" and wrote above it: "It's the only museum in which a painting has looked at me for half an hour without anyone disturbing us."

On the afternoon of the 23rd, Doina took Pietro and Giulia to a place no tourist ever entered: the costume store of the "Radu Stanca" National Theatre, where she had worked for forty years as an embroiderer. It was a large attic full of wardrobes, headless mannequins and costumes hanging by the hundred: kings, queens, peasants, ghosts, soldiers, angels. The old caretaker, who had known Doina for ever, greeted her with a bow. Doina went confidently to a wardrobe at the back, opened it and took out a dark red velvet cloak, embroidered with gold thread: leaves, birds, little stars. "I made this in 1979," she said. "For a King Lear. I was twenty-two. It took me four months." Pietro looked at the embroidery up close. Every leaf was made of hundreds of tiny stitches, all the same. "It's like a restoration," said Giulia quietly. Doina nodded. "The slower you do it," she said, "the better it comes out. And the less you see the hand, the more skilled the hand."

On Christmas Eve, while Doina was finishing the cooking, the doorbell rang. It was six children from the building, in woolly hats and with red cheeks, singing a slow, ancient song in several voices. Pietro didn't understand the words, but felt something tighten in his chest. Matei explained that they were colinde, the Christmas carols children take from house to house, receiving in exchange sweets, walnuts, apples, a few coins. "Just as at home you wish people well," he said, "here we sing it." Doina filled the children's hands with cozonac, the Christmas cake with walnuts, and Ion gave each of them a coin. Then the children sang another song, merrier, and one of them, the smallest, looked at Pietro and asked him something in Romanian. Matei translated, laughing: "He's asking whether in Italy children sing better than them." Pietro thought about it. "You tell him," he replied. "Not better. Different."

The next day, Pietro asked Ion to teach him a colind. Ion chose the simplest, "Florile dalbe", and made him repeat it twenty times in the kitchen, while Doina laughed at his pronunciation. Pietro understood almost nothing of the words, but learned the melody and the first two verses by heart, as he had learned Christmas poems for Graziella as a child. That evening, when the children of the building came back to sing at the doors, Pietro went out with them, in Ion's grey coat and a hat borrowed from Radu. They knocked on ten flats. At the third door, an elderly lady noticed that one of the carol singers was much taller than the others and sang with a strange accent. She asked him where he was from. "From Florence," Pietro answered in Romanian, the only sentence he could say well. The lady gave him twice as many walnuts as the other children. "For the journey," she said. Ion, waiting for him on the landing, laughed all evening.

At dinner Ilinca and Radu were there too, having come from Brașov with a cake and a bottle of pălincă. The table was so full you couldn't see the tablecloth: sarmale with sour cream and polenta, sausages, cheeses, pickles, chicken broth, the cozonac. Pietro tasted the sarmale, the famous cabbage rolls with meat and rice, cooked for hours. They were better than he expected, and heavier. Ion watched him closely. "Well?" he asked. "Are they better than ribollita?" It was the dangerous question, the one Pietro had asked him on the first day in the square. Everyone fell silent. Pietro understood that, whatever he answered, he would offend someone: Doina if he said no, Graziella if he said yes. So he did what he had learned in two years of debates, reviews and questions. "Sarmale aren't so much better than ribollita," he said, "as more… wintry. Ribollita is the soup of people who have little. Sarmale are the feast of people who have waited all year."

There was a moment's silence, then Ion burst out laughing and slapped the table, making the glasses tremble. "Diplomat!" he said in Romanian, and then in Italian: "You've got the makings of a foreign minister." Radu raised his glass of pălincă. "To Pietro," he said, "who has saved the peace between Tuscany and Transylvania." Everyone drank a toast. Doina, who hardly ever drank, took a sip and went red. Then she stood up, went into the kitchen and came back with a sheet folded in four. "For Graziella," she told Pietro. "The sarmale recipe. I've never given it to anyone outside the family. But Graziella is family now." Pietro put the sheet in the black notebook, between the Brukenthal pages. Later, when he opened it, he saw that at the bottom of the recipe Doina had added a line in Italian: "Secret ingredient: two per cent. Like the ribollita."

On Christmas Day, after lunch, Ion took Pietro for a walk in the old town, just the two of them, while the others slept. It was snowing gently, in big flakes. They walked in silence through the narrow streets, under the eyes of the roofs, to a small iron bridge, painted grey, which linked the upper town and the lower town. "This is the Podul Minciunilor," said Ion. "The Bridge of Lies. They say that if someone tells a lie while standing on it, the bridge collapses." Pietro looked at the bridge, which had been there since 1859 and didn't seem to have any intention of collapsing. "And it's never collapsed?" he asked. "Never," replied Ion. "Which means either the people of Sibiu are the most honest people in the world, or the legend is a lie too." He laughed. Then he became serious again. "Try it," he said. "Say something you think is true. Let's see if it holds."

Pietro stepped onto the bridge. He looked at the city under the snow, the red roofs turned white, the eyes of the houses half-closed under the snow like sleepy eyes. He thought of Florence, the Arno, the Ponte Vecchio, the trattoria. Then he said aloud, in Italian: "Florence is the most beautiful city in the world." The bridge didn't collapse. Ion laughed. "You see?" he said. "For you it's true. The bridge knows." Pietro stepped off the bridge, then stepped back on. This time he said: "Sibiu is more beautiful than Florence." The bridge, naturally, didn't collapse this time either. Pietro looked at Ion, puzzled. Ion came closer and put a hand on his shoulder, over the old grey wool coat that had been his. "That's the lesson of the bridge," he said. "When you compare two things you love, you never tell the truth or a lie. You only say where you are at that moment."

Walking home, through the snow, Ion told him a story he had never told even Matei. In 1990, a few months after the revolution, the railways had sent him to Italy on a training course, three weeks in Florence, in the Santa Maria Novella workshops. It was the first time he had left Romania. "I was more frightened than you can imagine," he said. "I didn't speak Italian, I had no money, and everything seemed bigger, richer, more beautiful than at home. For three weeks I compared everything. The trains, the streets, the bread, people's shoes. And every comparison made me feel smaller." He stopped under a street lamp, with the snow falling on his hat. "Then one evening an old stationmaster took me to eat in a trattoria in the Oltrarno. He made me taste a soup of bread and vegetables. And he told me: 'Don't compare. Eat.'"

Pietro stopped dead, in the middle of the street. "Which trattoria?" he asked. Ion smiled under his snow-white moustache. "I don't remember," he said. "It was long ago. A small trattoria, with checked tablecloths, in a narrow street near a bridge. There was a young woman in the kitchen, in a white apron, who never smiled but filled the plates to the brim." Pietro felt his heart pounding. In 1990 Graziella was thirty-six. Aldo was alive. The trattoria had existed for forty years. "The stationmaster," Pietro asked, his voice trembling, "was his name Franco?" Ion looked at him for a long time. Then he nodded. "Franco," he said. "When I came to Florence, before Viola was born, and they introduced him to me at the trattoria, it took us three glasses to realise we had already met, thirty years before. We decided not to tell anyone. A secret between railwaymen." Pietro couldn't say anything. Ion adjusted his hat. "I told you," he said quietly. "Don't compare. Look."

That night Pietro couldn't sleep. He phoned Graziella, even though it was late, and told her everything: Franco the stationmaster, 1990, the frightened Romanian railwayman, the bread soup. Graziella was silent for a long time. Then she said that yes, she remembered. Not the name, not the face. But she remembered that one spring evening in 1990 Franco, Signor Franco from the station, who came to eat with them every Thursday, had brought a foreign boy, very thin, who didn't speak and looked at everything with wide eyes. "He ate three plates of ribollita," said Graziella. "Aldo brought him a fourth without his asking. At the end the boy cried. We didn't understand why. Franco told us he came from a country where until a few months before there had been hunger." She paused. "Was it Ion?" Pietro said yes. Graziella said nothing for a while. Then she said only: "Then he's owed me the sarmale for thirty-eight years."

The last days passed faster than Pietro would have liked. He went skating on the frozen lake in the park with Viola, who fell eighteen times and laughed eighteen times. He climbed the Council Tower and counted the eyes on the roofs: he stopped at two hundred and forty, because it was too cold. He ate kürtőskalács at the market, a tube-shaped cake baked on a spit, and decided it was the best cake he had ever tasted, then felt guilty towards Graziella's tiramisù. On New Year's Eve, at midnight, he watched the fireworks from Doina's window, with Ion beside him checking the time on his silver watch. "Midnight," said Ion, closing the lid. "Exactly. This watch hasn't been a minute wrong in forty years. Like the railwaymen of old."

On 2 January they flew back to Florence. At the airport, Ion hugged Pietro longer than he had hugged Matei, and Doina gave him a parcel wrapped in newspaper: inside was a small embroidered tablecloth, with gold leaves and birds on a red ground, the same as on King Lear's cloak. "For the trattoria," she said. "For Bellini's table." Pietro wanted to give back the grey wool coat, but Ion shook his head. "Keep it," he said. "You don't need it in Florence, I know. But one day you'll be cold somewhere, in some city you don't know, and you'll compare everything with home. Then put it on, and remember the bridge." Pietro put it on again, even though it was warm in the airport. Viola, in Matei's arms, waved to her grandparents until they disappeared behind passport control.

At the trattoria, on the evening of their return, Graziella was waiting with ribollita on the table and a question ready. She waited for Pietro to take off his coat, sit down, eat two spoonfuls. Then she asked, hands on her hips: "Well. Is Sibiu more beautiful than Florence?" The whole trattoria turned to listen. Pietro put down his spoon. He thought about it, as he had on the bridge. "It isn't so much more beautiful," he said, "as more… far away. And the further away it is, the more it resembles home." Graziella looked at him with narrowed eyes, as she did when tasting a new sauce. Then Pietro took the sheet folded in four out of his bag and gave it to her. "From Doina," he said. "The sarmale recipe. And from Ion: thank you for the fourth ribollita, in 1990." Graziella read the sheet. She read the last line, the one about the two per cent. Then she turned towards the kitchen, in silence, and nobody saw whether she was crying.

Doina's embroidered tablecloth was put that very evening on Bellini's table, and when he saw it he took off his glasses and touched it with his fingertips, as you touch an old canvas. "Painted stitch," he said. "Done by hand. It takes months." Graziella announced that the following Thursday, in honour of Franco and Ion, the trattoria would serve sarmale, for the first time in almost eighty years of history. She cooked them following the recipe word for word, except for the two per cent, which she added her own way and revealed to no one. The customers said they were delicious. Old Signor Franco, who was ninety and still came every Thursday, ate two plates, then asked Pietro to send a photo of the dish to Sibiu. Pietro sent it. Ten minutes later Ion's reply arrived, in Italian: "Better than ours. Don't tell Doina."

In the black notebook, on the page for 2 January, Pietro wrote the conclusion of the trip. He reread the two pages from the first day, the ones full of "more" and "less", and struck them through with a light line, without erasing them, as Ruggeri had taught him to do with wrong hypotheses. Below he wrote: "On the first day I compared everything, and saw nothing. On the second day I looked at a painting for half an hour without comparing it with any other, and I really saw it. Ion was right: comparing is the easiest way not to look." Then he added a line, the last, in small letters: "Sibiu is neither more nor less beautiful than Florence. It's more Sibiu." He reread the sentence and it seemed strange to him, almost wrong in Italian. Then he thought of the Bridge of Lies, which would certainly have held up under that sentence, and left it as it was.
